I have farmed this 2.6 mu for 20 years, and with my husband working off-farm and the children in school, I manage the fields mostly by myself. On a small plot like mine, leaving land idle is not an option, so I stick to the wheat-maize double crop that everyone in Quzhou relies on. I will plant all 2.6 mu to improved wheat in October because the local supply store stocks varieties that have done well here for years, and I trust what I know. For the summer maize, I always buy hybrid seed—yes, it costs more, but the yield jump is worth every yuan on this tiny farm. I have my own well, so I can irrigate when I need to, but the pump runs on electricity and I must save where I can; I will water wheat three times at the crucial stages before winter, at jointing, and during filling, and maize twice because summer rain sometimes helps but I cannot count on it. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer at sowing and follow with urea topdressing. I give wheat a bit more nitrogen and phosphorus since it is the main staple and must survive the cold, while maize gets a moderate dose to push grain filling without wasting money. Pests and weeds can wipe out a smallholder fast, so I spray twice per crop: once to control weeds and once for insects. Before wheat, I rotary till to chop in the maize stubble and level the seedbed. After wheat harvest in early June, the window to plant maize is narrow, so I use no-tillage seeding straight into the stubble to save time and keep soil moisture. If the weather does not play tricks, I expect about 450 kg per mu from the wheat and 550 kg per mu from the maize.
